title: Starting your family tree
lead: Five steps to begin your research and complete family history charts.

video.label: The five steps in a minute and a half

before.heading: Your family tree
questions: Why do you want to trace it?
Who could benefit from what you discover?

steps.title: Write down what you know
steps.question: What do I know?
points: Look through family homes and Bibles
Record details on pedigree charts and family group records

steps.title: Decide what you want to learn
steps.question: What do I want to know?
text: Start with the generation closest to you. Work back one generation at a time.
Turn gaps in your knowledge into specific research questions.

groups.title: Records and documents
groups.text: Census, military and emigration records; microfilms; FamilySearch.org

groups.title: People and objects
groups.text: Relatives, family friends, photographs and tombstones

steps.title: Learn from the resource
steps.question: What did I learn?
points: Study and copy details from the object

steps.title: Use the information
points: Evaluate and organise what you found
Add it to your family tree or begin the five steps again
Share it with relatives and other researchers

charts.heading: Completing charts
charts.lead: Pedigree charts and family group records

record.title: Record the details clearly
points: Use a pencil until you are certain of the facts.
Write surnames in capitals: Gordon (given name), GORDON (surname).
Use a three-letter month name to avoid date ambiguity.
record.note: For example, 04/05/1925 can mean 4 May or 5 April 1925.

numbering.title: Follow the numbering
numbering.note: Complete the nearest generation as fully as you can before moving back. Missing details can lead to the wrong tree.

family.title: Family group records
points: Complete one record for each couple with children.
Use “Other Spouses” to indicate additional children with another partner.
Apply the same surname and date formatting rules.

cta.heading: Stuck? Bring it to a meeting
cta.text: Bring your charts and your questions. Someone at the table has usually been stuck in the same place, and your first visit is free.
